title: Database Security & Emerging Trends
intro: Access control, encryption, auditing, NoSQL, big data and blockchain.

sec.s: A database is a structured collection of data managed by a database management system (DBMS).

b.x: A database is a structured collection of data managed by a database management system (DBMS). Databases may store student records, financial transactions, customer details, medical records, product inventories, login information, and many other types of information. Because databases often contain valuable or confidential data, protecting them is a fundamental part of software and system design.

Database security refers to the policies, procedures, and technical controls used to protect data against unauthorized access, misuse, disclosure, alteration, destruction, and interruption. Security applies not only to the database software itself but also to the applications, accounts, networks, operating systems, storage systems, and people that interact with it.

Consider a college database. Students may be allowed to view their own results, teachers may be allowed to enter marks for assigned courses, and administrators may manage student registration. If every user receives unrestricted access to every table, an ordinary account could change grades or read private records. Access control limits what each identity can do.

Encryption protects data in situations where an attacker might obtain access to a storage device, backup file, or network traffic. Auditing records relevant activities so that suspicious events can be investigated. Monitoring helps identify attacks or operational problems as they happen.

Modern database systems also face different scaling requirements. Traditional relational databases use tables and structured schemas. NoSQL systems may use documents, key-value records, wide-column structures, or graphs. Distributed databases spread data across multiple machines, while Big Data technologies process large, fast, or diverse datasets. Blockchain systems maintain a shared ledger through a distributed protocol and cryptographic techniques.

These technologies solve different problems. NoSQL is not automatically more secure or faster than SQL, Big Data is not a single database product, and blockchain is not a universal replacement for a conventional database. Choosing a technology requires understanding its data model, consistency guarantees, workload, security requirements, operational cost, and failure behavior.
Learning objectives

x: Explain database security and common threats.
Distinguish authentication from authorization.
Describe Discretionary Access Control (DAC) and Role-Based Access Control (RBAC).
Explain encryption at rest and encryption in transit.
Understand database auditing, monitoring, and suspicious-access detection.
Introduce NoSQL, MongoDB, and Apache Cassandra.
Explain the CAP theorem in distributed systems.
Describe Big Data characteristics and technologies.
Explain blockchain and its role as a distributed ledger.
Compare these approaches and identify their limitations.

sec.s: A common framework for information security is the CIA triad: Confidentiality, Integrity, and Availability.

b.x: 2.1 The CIA triad
A common framework for information security is the CIA triad: Confidentiality, Integrity, and Availability.
Confidentiality
Only authorized users and systems should access protected information.

x: A student should not be able to read another student's private academic or contact details unless the application grants that permission.

b.x: Integrity
Data should remain accurate, complete, and protected from unauthorized or improper modification.

x: An unauthorized user should not be able to change a student's grade or alter a bank balance without an authorized transaction.

b.x: Availability
Authorized users should be able to access the database when needed.

x: A hospital system should remain available to authorized clinical staff, subject to its resilience and recovery requirements.

b.x: Security controls often support more than one goal. Encryption supports confidentiality; integrity checks and access controls protect integrity; backups and resilient architecture support availability.
2.2 Authentication
Authentication answers: “Who or what are you?”
It verifies the identity of a user, service, device, or application. Common authentication methods include:

x: Passwords.
One-time codes.
Security keys.
Certificates.
Biometrics, usually as part of a broader authentication system.
Multi-factor authentication (MFA).

b.x: A database account may authenticate using a password, certificate, or an identity system integrated with the organization's infrastructure.
2.3 Authorization
Authorization answers: “What are you allowed to do?”

After identity has been established, authorization decides which operations the identity may perform. Permissions can include reading, inserting, updating, deleting, creating tables, managing users, or administering the database.
Authentication and authorization are related but different. A user can authenticate successfully and still be denied access to a particular table.
2.4 Common database threats
Unauthorized access
An attacker or unapproved user obtains access to data or functions.
Privilege abuse
A legitimate account uses permissions in an inappropriate way, intentionally or accidentally.
SQL injection
An application places untrusted input into SQL commands in a way that changes the intended query structure.
Credential theft
Passwords, tokens, or keys are stolen and used to impersonate an authorized identity.
Data exposure
Sensitive information is exposed through an insecure backup, misconfigured cloud storage, logs, an application error, or a poorly protected database endpoint.
Insider threat
An employee, contractor, administrator, or other trusted person misuses access or mishandles data.
Malware and ransomware
Malicious software may steal, encrypt, destroy, or disrupt access to data.
Denial of service
Excessive or malicious requests exhaust database resources and prevent legitimate use.
Misconfiguration
Default credentials, excessive permissions, open network access, disabled security features, or poorly protected backups create vulnerabilities.
Unpatched software
Known vulnerabilities remain exploitable because database software, drivers, operating systems, or applications are not updated.
2.5 Defense in depth
Defense in depth means using multiple complementary layers rather than relying on one control.
A database security plan may include

x: Strong identity verification.
Least-privilege access.
Network segmentation and firewall rules.
Encryption at rest and in transit.
Parameterized queries.
Auditing and alerting.
Regular patching.
Secure backups.
Recovery testing.
Incident-response procedures.

b.x: If one layer fails, other layers may still limit damage or reveal the attack.

sec.s: Access control defines who can access which resources and which actions they can perform.

b.x: Access control defines who can access which resources and which actions they can perform.
A database contains resources such as

x: Databases and schemas.
Tables and views.
Rows or columns, where supported.
Stored procedures and functions.
Sequences and other database objects.
Administrative operations.

b.x: Typical permissions include

x: SELECT: read data.
INSERT: add rows.
UPDATE: modify rows.
DELETE: remove rows.
EXECUTE: run an authorized procedure or function.
CREATE: create particular objects.
ALTER: change object definitions.
DROP: remove objects.
GRANT: give privileges to other identities, where permitted.

b.x: Exact privilege names and scopes vary across DBMS products.
3.1 Principle of least privilege
The principle of least privilege says that each user, application, and service should receive only the permissions needed for its responsibilities.
For example

x: A reporting account may need read-only access to selected views.
An application account may need SELECT, INSERT, and UPDATE on particular tables but not permission to create users or drop the database.
A database administrator may need broader privileges, but administrative access should be limited and monitored.

b.x: Least privilege reduces the damage caused by mistakes, compromised accounts, and malicious activity.
3.2 Default deny
Default deny means access is blocked unless an explicit rule permits it. This is generally safer than granting broad access and trying to remove every dangerous permission afterward.
3.3 Separation of duties

Separation of duties divides sensitive responsibilities among different people or accounts. For example, the person who requests a financial adjustment may not be the same person who approves it. In database administration, ordinary application accounts should generally not have unrestricted administrative capabilities.
3.4 Grant and revoke
Many relational DBMSs provide GRANT and REVOKE statements to manage privileges. The exact syntax and supported privilege types depend on the product.
Illustrative SQL

x: GRANT SELECT ON Student TO reporting_user;
REVOKE SELECT ON Student FROM reporting_user;

b.x: This is conceptual syntax; some products use different user, role, schema, or object naming rules. Always check the target DBMS's documentation before applying security changes.

sec.s: Discretionary Access Control (DAC) is an access-control model in which resource owners or authorized users…

b.x: 4.1 Definition
Discretionary Access Control (DAC) is an access-control model in which resource owners or authorized users can grant or revoke access to resources, subject to the system's rules.
In a database, the creator or owner of an object may be able to grant permissions to other users. An administrator may also have authority to assign permissions.
“Discretionary” means the permissions can be assigned or delegated by an authorized owner or controller; it does not mean that access is uncontrolled or that any user can do anything.
4.2 How DAC works
A simplified DAC process

x: A user authenticates.
The DBMS identifies the requested object and operation.
The system checks the user's privileges and applicable rules.
The operation is allowed or denied.
Relevant events may be recorded in audit logs.

b.x: For example, a teacher owns or manages a course-results table and is authorized to grant a teaching assistant read-only access. The assistant can view the relevant data but cannot change grades if no update privilege was granted.
4.3 Access control lists
An access control list (ACL) associates a resource with users or groups and the permissions they hold.
Resource: COURSE_RESULTS

x: Teacher A: SELECT, UPDATE
Teaching Assistant: SELECT
Auditor: SELECT
Student App: SELECT on an approved view only

b.x: This is an illustrative representation, not a specific DBMS's ACL syntax.
4.4 Advantages of DAC
Flexibility
Owners can share resources without requiring every permission change to pass through a central administrator.
Convenience
Access can be adjusted to meet changing collaboration needs.
Fine-grained control
Depending on the DBMS, permissions can be granted on specific objects and sometimes more granular scopes.
Compatibility
Many traditional database privilege systems support owner- or administrator-controlled grants.
4.5 Disadvantages of DAC
Privilege propagation
Permissions may be delegated or spread in ways that are difficult to track.
Human error
A user may accidentally grant more access than intended.
Inconsistent policies
Different owners may make inconsistent decisions.
Insider risk
A user with legitimate control over an object may share it inappropriately.
Complexity
As users and objects grow, permission management can become difficult.
4.6 Example scenario

A student project team maintains a shared database. The project leader owns a table and grants team members permission to read it. One member later grants access to another account if the DBMS permits that delegation and the member has the necessary grant option.
The flexibility is useful, but the team must ensure that permissions are not extended to unintended users. Organizations often limit delegation for sensitive data.
4.7 DAC is not the same as unrestricted access

DAC still relies on authenticated identities, permissions, and enforcement by the DBMS. Its defining characteristic is the discretionary ability to grant or revoke access, not the absence of security.

sec.s: Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) assigns permissions to roles and then assigns users or service identities…

b.x: 5.1 Definition

Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) assigns permissions to roles and then assigns users or service identities to those roles. Rather than giving every user a custom collection of permissions, the organization defines roles around job functions or responsibilities.
Example roles

x: Student.
Teacher.
Registrar.
Reporting Analyst.
Application Service.
Database Administrator.
Security Auditor.

b.x: A role is a named collection of permissions. A user assigned to that role receives those permissions according to the DBMS's role model.
5.2 How RBAC works
Typical process

x: Define the roles.
Grant permissions to each role.
Assign users or service accounts to appropriate roles.
Review role membership periodically.
Remove or adjust membership when responsibilities change.
Audit privileged roles and sensitive operations.

b.x: For example, a Reporting Analyst role may be granted SELECT access to approved views but no direct access to tables containing unnecessary personal information.
5.3 Illustrative role example
Role: STUDENT_ROLE

x: View approved course information.
View the current user's permitted academic information through application-controlled access.

b.x: Role: TEACHER_ROLE

x: Read assigned course rosters.
Enter or update marks for assigned courses, subject to application and database rules.

b.x: Role: AUDITOR_ROLE

x: Read audit records and selected reports.
No permission to modify ordinary academic data.

b.x: Role: DB_ADMIN_ROLE

x: Manage database objects and selected administrative tasks.
Use only through restricted administrative identities and with appropriate monitoring.

b.x: Real DBMS role syntax and the ability to restrict row-level access vary. A role name alone does not guarantee that a user can access only their own rows. Row-level security, views, application logic, and database policies may also be required.
5.4 Role hierarchy

Some RBAC systems support role inheritance. A senior role may inherit the permissions of a more basic role. For example, a department manager might inherit ordinary reporting permissions plus additional approval permissions.
Role hierarchy can reduce duplication, but inheritance must be designed carefully. A mistakenly broad parent role can expose sensitive permissions to many users.
5.5 Separation of duties in RBAC

RBAC can help enforce separation of duties. For example, one role may prepare a payment and another may approve it. A system can be designed to prevent one identity from holding both roles where that would violate policy.

Static separation of duties limits which roles may be assigned to one user. Dynamic separation of duties limits which roles may be used together in a particular session or transaction. The precise capabilities depend on the system implementing RBAC.
5.6 Advantages of RBAC
Scalability
Permissions can be managed by job function rather than separately for every user.
Consistency
Users with the same responsibilities can receive the same permission set.
Simpler onboarding
Assigning a user to a suitable role can provide the necessary access.
Simpler offboarding
Removing a role or disabling an account can remove access through that role.
Auditing
It is easier to explain why a user has a permission when the permission is tied to a documented role.
Least privilege
Well-designed roles can limit users to the minimum access required.
5.7 Disadvantages of RBAC
Role explosion
Too many narrowly defined roles can make management difficult.
Incorrect role design
An overly broad role can give many users excessive permissions.
Stale membership
Users may retain roles after changing jobs unless membership is reviewed.
Limited context by itself
Traditional RBAC may not express every contextual rule, such as access only from a managed device during a particular period. Additional policy mechanisms may be needed.
5.8 DAC versus RBAC
DAC focuses on discretionary grants associated with resources and authorized owners or controllers.
RBAC focuses on assigning permissions to roles and assigning identities to those roles.

They are not always mutually exclusive. A DBMS may support object grants and role-based privilege assignment together. Administrators may use roles for standard job functions while applying additional grants or policies for special cases.

sec.t: DAC and RBAC: Comparison and Best Practices

x: Feature | DAC | RBAC
Main basis | Owner/controller grants | Roles and job responsibilities
Permission assignment | Often object-specific grants | Permissions assigned to roles, then users assigned to roles
Flexibility | Can be flexible for resource sharing | Consistent across users with similar duties
Scalability | Individual grants can become complex | Roles simplify large-scale administration when designed well
Common risk | Uncontrolled or excessive delegation | Overly broad roles or role explosion
Best fit | Situations requiring owner-controlled sharing | Organizations with repeatable job functions
Can coexist? | Yes | Yes

b.x: 6.1 Best practices for access control

x: Apply least privilege.
Use separate accounts for people, applications, and administrative tasks.
Avoid shared accounts where individual accountability is required.
Use roles for standard responsibilities.
Restrict the ability to grant privileges to other users.
Review privileged accounts and role memberships regularly.
Disable or remove unused accounts.
Use read-only views for reporting where practical.
Apply row-level or column-level controls when required and supported.
Test access rules using both permitted and prohibited operations.
Record and review sensitive administrative actions.
Keep development, test, and production access appropriately separated.

sec.s: Encryption transforms readable information, called plaintext, into an encoded form, called ciphertext,…

b.x: 7.1 What is encryption?

Encryption transforms readable information, called plaintext, into an encoded form, called ciphertext, using a cryptographic algorithm and a key. Decryption uses the appropriate key to recover readable data.
The main purpose of encryption is to prevent parties without the required key from reading protected information.

Encryption is not a replacement for authorization. An application may decrypt data after a user has authenticated, so a compromised application account could still expose plaintext if it has broad access.
7.2 Symmetric encryption
Symmetric encryption uses the same secret key, or closely related key material, for encryption and decryption.
Advantages

x: Efficient for large amounts of data.
Commonly used to encrypt files, disks, backups, and network sessions.

b.x: Challenges

x: The key must be protected.
Authorized systems need a secure way to obtain the key.
A leaked key may expose all data protected by it.

b.x: Modern systems use established algorithms and libraries rather than designing their own encryption schemes.
7.3 Asymmetric cryptography

Asymmetric cryptography uses a public key and a private key. Public-key techniques are commonly used for identity verification, digital signatures, and establishing shared secrets. They can help set up secure connections without directly sharing a long-term secret key.
For bulk data, secure protocols generally use hybrid cryptography: asymmetric techniques help establish or authenticate the session, while symmetric encryption protects the main data stream.
7.4 Encryption versus hashing
Encryption is designed to be reversible with the correct key.

A cryptographic hash maps input data to a fixed-size digest and is not intended to be reversed. Hashes are useful for integrity checks and other purposes. Password storage should use a purpose-built password-hashing scheme with a salt and suitable work factor, not ordinary reversible encryption and not a fast general-purpose hash alone.
7.5 Encryption versus encoding
Encoding, such as Base64, changes the representation of data but does not provide confidentiality. Anyone can decode it without a secret key. Encoding should never be treated as encryption.
7.6 What encryption does not automatically solve
Encryption does not necessarily prevent

x: An authorized but malicious user from reading data.
An application vulnerability from exposing decrypted information.
Ransomware from damaging accessible files.
A stolen application session from being misused.
Data loss when keys are destroyed or lost.
Metadata leakage, such as access patterns or record sizes.

b.x: Encryption should be combined with access control, secure software, monitoring, key management, and backups.

sec.s: Data at rest is data stored on a persistent medium rather than actively travelling through a communication…

b.x: 8.1 Definition
Data at rest is data stored on a persistent medium rather than actively travelling through a communication channel. Examples include:

x: Database data files.
Transaction logs.
Backups.
Exported files.
Snapshots.
Storage volumes.
Portable storage devices.

b.x: Encryption at rest protects stored information if someone obtains the storage media or files without having the required decryption key.
8.2 Full-disk or volume encryption
Full-disk or volume encryption protects a storage device or volume. The operating system or storage layer decrypts data for authorized use.
Advantages

x: Can protect many files without modifying each application.
Helps protect lost or stolen devices and improperly accessed storage media.

b.x: Limitations

x: Once the system is running and the volume is unlocked, a sufficiently privileged attacker may access data through the operating system.
It may not independently protect against an authorized database user who can query plaintext.
Key storage and boot configuration must be managed securely.

b.x: 8.3 Database-level encryption
Some database products support encryption of database files or selected database structures. The implementation may protect database pages, logs, backups, or particular fields.

The exact feature is product-specific. Database-level encryption can integrate with database administration and key management, but administrators must understand which files and operations are covered.
8.4 Transparent Data Encryption (TDE)

Transparent Data Encryption is a term used by several DBMS products for encryption of database files at the storage layer. Applications and authorized database queries can continue to work without explicitly encrypting and decrypting every field in application code.

TDE can protect database files and backups in supported configurations, but it does not automatically hide data from users who are authorized to query the database. It also does not replace network encryption, access control, or careful backup-key management.
8.5 Column-level or field-level encryption

Sensitive columns, such as government identifiers or selected financial information, may be encrypted separately. Field-level encryption can limit exposure if a user can access the table but should not see the protected value.
Challenges include

x: Key distribution and rotation.
Searching or sorting encrypted values.
Indexing limitations.
Application complexity.
Preventing accidental plaintext leakage through logs or error messages.

b.x: Some applications use tokenization, where sensitive values are replaced with tokens and the original values are stored in a separately protected system.
8.6 Backup encryption

Backups may contain a complete copy of sensitive data, so they require protection comparable to the live database. Encryption should cover backup files and transferred backup copies, with access to decryption keys restricted and recovery procedures tested.
A backup encrypted with a lost key may be unusable. Key recovery and secure escrow procedures should be planned before an incident occurs.
8.7 Benefits of encryption at rest

x: Reduces risk from stolen disks or improperly accessed storage files.
Protects backup and snapshot contents when configured correctly.
Helps meet security policies and regulatory requirements.
Limits exposure from some physical and storage-layer attacks.

b.x: 8.8 Limitations and best practices

x: Restrict access to encryption keys.
Keep keys separate from the encrypted data where feasible.
Use supported, modern cryptographic implementations.
Encrypt backups and exported files.
Monitor access to key-management systems.
Rotate keys according to policy and risk.
Test restoration using the required keys.
Do not assume that at-rest encryption protects data from every database administrator or application-level attack.

sec.s: Data in transit is data moving between systems over a network or communication channel.

b.x: 9.1 Definition
Data in transit is data moving between systems over a network or communication channel. Examples include:

x: An application connecting to a database server.
A database replica communicating with another node.
A client downloading a report.
A backup being transferred to remote storage.
An administrator connecting to a database management endpoint.

b.x: Without suitable transport protection, network traffic may be exposed to eavesdropping or modification.
9.2 TLS
Transport Layer Security (TLS) is widely used to protect network communications. Correctly configured TLS can provide:

x: Confidentiality through encryption.
Integrity protection against undetected modification.
Authentication of the server and, where configured, the client.

b.x: HTTPS is HTTP carried over TLS. Database drivers may also support TLS-protected database connections.
9.3 Certificate validation

A secure connection requires more than merely turning on encryption. The client should verify that the server certificate is valid and identifies the intended server according to the configured trust model.
If certificate validation is disabled or bypassed, an attacker may be able to impersonate the server even if the connection is encrypted.
9.4 Mutual TLS
Mutual TLS (mTLS) authenticates both sides of a connection using certificates. It is useful for service-to-service communication where both the client and server must establish their identities.
mTLS can reduce reliance on passwords for some service connections, but certificates, private keys, and trust policies must be managed securely.
9.5 Common risks

x: Using plaintext connections across untrusted networks.
Disabling certificate verification.
Allowing outdated or weak protocol configurations.
Failing to encrypt replication or backup traffic.
Exposing database ports directly to the public internet.
Logging connection secrets or credentials.

b.x: 9.6 Best practices for transit encryption

x: Require TLS for remote database connections when supported.
Validate certificates correctly.
Use current, supported TLS configurations.
Protect client and server private keys.
Restrict network access with firewalls and private networking.
Use separate network policies for administrative and application traffic.
Protect replication and backup traffic as well as ordinary queries.
Monitor certificate expiration and connection failures.

sec.s: Encryption is only as strong operationally as the protection around its keys.

b.x: 10.1 Why key management matters

Encryption is only as strong operationally as the protection around its keys. If an attacker steals a key, encrypted data may become readable. If the organization loses the key, legitimate recovery may become impossible.
Key management includes key generation, storage, access control, distribution, rotation, revocation, backup, recovery, and destruction.
10.2 Key hierarchy
A system may use a hierarchy of keys. For example

x: A key-encryption key protects other keys.
A data-encryption key encrypts database data.
A master key protects the data-encryption key.

b.x: The specific hierarchy varies by product. Separating key-encryption and data-encryption roles can simplify rotation and reduce exposure.
10.3 Key storage
Keys may be managed by

x: A dedicated key-management service.
A hardware security module (HSM).
A protected operating-system keystore.
A secrets-management system.

b.x: Keys should not be casually stored in source code, public repositories, unsecured configuration files, or the same unprotected location as the data they protect.
10.4 Rotation and revocation
Key rotation replaces a key or changes which key is used for new encryption. Some systems re-encrypt old data; others maintain multiple key versions so that older data can still be decrypted.
Revocation removes or restricts trust in a key or certificate that is compromised or no longer valid.
A rotation plan should consider old backups, archived logs, replicas, and disaster-recovery copies. A key cannot simply be deleted if it is still needed to restore retained data.
10.5 Access control and auditing for keys

Only authorized services and people should be able to use or administer encryption keys. Key-management operations should be logged and reviewed, especially key export, policy changes, deletion, and unusual access attempts.

sec.s: Database auditing is the recording of selected activities so that the organization can establish what…

b.x: 11.1 Auditing definition

Database auditing is the recording of selected activities so that the organization can establish what happened, when it happened, which identity was involved, and which objects or operations were affected.
Audit records may include

x: Successful and failed login attempts.
Account creation and deletion.
Privilege grants and revocations.
Access to sensitive tables or views.
Changes to schema objects.
Administrative operations.
Data modifications.
Changes to audit settings.
Unexpected or denied actions.

b.x: The exact events available depend on the DBMS and its configuration.
11.2 Auditing versus monitoring
Auditing focuses on creating a record for accountability, investigation, and compliance.

Monitoring analyzes events and system metrics to identify suspicious behavior, errors, performance issues, or policy violations. Monitoring may use audit logs, database logs, network telemetry, operating-system events, and application logs.
The two functions overlap but are not identical. An audit record can exist without an immediate alert; monitoring can use metrics that are not part of the formal audit trail.
11.3 Why auditing matters
Accountability
A record helps determine which account performed an action.
Incident investigation
Logs can show a sequence of events before and after a suspected compromise.
Compliance
Organizations may need evidence that sensitive operations are recorded and reviewed.
Threat detection
Repeated failed logins, unusual data exports, or unexpected privilege changes may indicate an attack.
Operational troubleshooting
Audit and event data can help explain unexpected changes, subject to appropriate privacy and retention controls.
11.4 What should be audited?
Potential high-value events include

x: Authentication successes and failures.
Access to highly sensitive tables.
Changes to permissions and roles.
Creation of privileged accounts.
Disabling of logging or monitoring.
Bulk data exports.
Schema changes in production.
Unusual deletes or mass updates.
Changes to backup, encryption, or key settings.

b.x: Audit selection should be risk-based. Recording every query indiscriminately may create large costs and may capture unnecessary sensitive information.
11.5 Audit-log protection
Audit logs should be protected from unauthorized modification or deletion. Helpful controls include:

x: Restricting write and read access.
Sending logs to a separate logging system.
Applying retention and integrity controls.
Synchronizing clocks across systems.
Monitoring for missing log events.
Separating the administrator who manages the database from the person who reviews security logs where feasible.

b.x: If a compromised database administrator can erase every audit record on the same system, the audit trail may be unreliable. External or separately controlled log storage helps reduce that risk.

sec.s: One indicator does not always prove an attack.

b.x: 12.1 Common indicators
Potential warning signs include

x: Many failed logins from one source.
Login attempts against many usernames.
Logins at unusual times or from unfamiliar locations.
Use of disabled or expired accounts.
A normal account attempting administrative actions.
Unexpected privilege escalation.
Repeated attempts to access restricted tables.
Large or unusual exports.
Sudden changes to audit configuration.
A service account connecting from an unexpected host.
Database connections from an unapproved network.

b.x: One indicator does not always prove an attack. For example, a burst of failed logins may result from a misconfigured application. Alerts should be investigated in context.
12.2 Login-failure monitoring
A monitoring rule might alert when a single account or source produces an unusual number of failed authentication attempts within a defined period.

The threshold should reflect the environment. A small internal system and a public service may require different thresholds. Detection systems should also consider distributed attempts that use many source addresses.
12.3 Privilege-change monitoring
Changes to user accounts, roles, grants, and administrative policies should be treated as high-value events. Unexpected changes may indicate compromise or a mistake.
Useful questions include

x: Who made the change?
Was it approved?
Which permissions were added or removed?
Was the change made through the normal administrative process?
Did the account subsequently access sensitive data?

b.x: 12.4 Unusual data-access monitoring
Examples of potentially suspicious activity

x: A reporting account reads far more rows than usual.
A service accesses tables unrelated to its function.
A user downloads a large amount of sensitive information.
A query scans sensitive records at an unusual time.
A previously inactive account becomes active.

b.x: Detection can combine audit logs with normal usage baselines. A baseline should not be treated as proof of legitimacy: an attacker may imitate ordinary behavior.
12.5 Avoiding sensitive data in logs

Logs should normally record enough information to investigate an event without copying unnecessary sensitive content. Avoid recording passwords, authentication tokens, encryption keys, or complete sensitive records unless there is a carefully justified and protected need.
A query log containing personal data may itself become a security and privacy risk. Use masking, redaction, access restrictions, and retention limits.
12.6 Example monitoring workflow

x: Collect authentication, audit, and database events.
Normalize timestamps and identity information.
Apply rules or analytics to identify unusual patterns.
Create an alert with relevant context.
Verify whether the event is authorized or expected.
Contain a suspected compromise using an approved process.
Preserve evidence.
Reset or revoke compromised credentials when appropriate.
Investigate the cause and scope.
Document findings and improve controls.

b.x: 12.7 Incident response
A practical incident-response process often includes
Preparation
Define responsibilities, contact paths, access controls, and response procedures.
Detection and analysis
Validate alerts, identify affected accounts and systems, and determine likely scope.
Containment
Limit ongoing access or damage, for example by disabling a compromised account or restricting network paths. Actions should consider operational safety and evidence preservation.
Eradication
Remove the cause, such as a vulnerable component or compromised credential.
Recovery
Restore trusted operation, validate integrity, and monitor closely.
Lessons learned
Document what happened, why controls failed, and which improvements are needed.

The appropriate response depends on the severity and the system's business requirements. Avoid making destructive changes before preserving required evidence and coordinating with responsible administrators.

sec.t: Security Monitoring, Alerts, and Incident Response
sec.s: A SIEM platform collects and correlates events from different systems, such as databases, applications,…

b.x: 13.1 Security Information and Event Management (SIEM)

A SIEM platform collects and correlates events from different systems, such as databases, applications, identity providers, operating systems, and network devices. It can apply rules and analytics to identify suspicious combinations of events.
For example, a SIEM may correlate

x: Several failed logins.
A successful login from an unusual source.
A privilege change.
A large data export soon afterward.

b.x: Together, these events may be more concerning than any one event alone.
13.2 Metrics and database health
Monitoring should include both security and reliability. Relevant metrics may include:

x: Connection counts.
Query errors.
Authentication failures.
CPU, memory, storage, and I/O usage.
Replication lag.
Backup success and restore-test results.
Lock waits and deadlocks.
Unusual query volume.
Database availability and recovery time.

b.x: A performance incident can sometimes be caused by malicious traffic, but high resource use is not automatically evidence of an attack.
13.3 Alert quality
Too many false alerts cause alert fatigue. Useful alerts should have:

x: A clear description of the event.
Severity and confidence.
Relevant user, source, object, and timestamp information.
A suggested investigation path.
An assigned owner or response process.

b.x: Alerts should be tested and reviewed as system usage changes.
13.4 Retention and privacy

Audit retention should meet legal, operational, and security requirements while avoiding unnecessary storage of sensitive information. Long retention can help investigations but increases storage costs and the impact of a log compromise.

sec.s: Relational databases organize information into tables of rows and columns.

b.x: 14.1 Relational databases
Relational databases organize information into tables of rows and columns. They commonly use SQL and support relationships through keys and constraints.
Examples include PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, Microsoft SQL Server, and Oracle Database.
Strengths often include

x: Structured schemas.
Joins and expressive queries.
Constraints and transactions.
Mature reporting and analytics tools.
Strong support for relational data and integrity rules.

b.x: They can also scale to large workloads using a variety of techniques, including indexing, replication, partitioning, and distributed architectures. It is incorrect to assume that all relational databases are limited to small or single-server applications.
14.2 What is NoSQL?
NoSQL is a broad term for database systems that do not rely exclusively on the traditional relational-table model. The term is often expanded as “Not Only SQL.”
NoSQL systems may be designed around flexible schemas, specific access patterns, horizontal scaling, distributed availability, or data structures that differ from relational tables.
Common categories include:
Document databases
Store records as document-like structures, often using JSON-like formats.
Key-value databases
Store values indexed by keys.
Wide-column databases
Organize data into rows and column families or related wide-column structures.
Graph databases
Represent entities as nodes and relationships as edges.
NoSQL does not mean “no query language,” “no transactions,” or “no consistency.” Many NoSQL systems provide query languages, transactions of varying scope, and configurable consistency guarantees.
14.3 Why use NoSQL?
Potential reasons include

x: Flexible or evolving data structures.
High-volume distributed workloads.
Access patterns that fit document, key-value, wide-column, or graph models.
Horizontal scaling across nodes.
Low-latency reads or writes for particular workloads.
Data models that naturally represent nested documents or relationships.

b.x: Possible trade-offs include

x: More application responsibility for data relationships.
Different transaction semantics.
Denormalized data and duplicated values.
Query limitations or workload-specific data modeling.
More operational complexity in distributed deployments.

b.x: NoSQL is not automatically a better choice. Select the system based on data shape, query patterns, consistency requirements, operational skills, and cost.

sec.s: MongoDB is a document-oriented database.

b.x: 15.1 What is MongoDB?

MongoDB is a document-oriented database. It stores records as BSON documents, a binary-encoded document format that supports fields and nested structures. Its data model can represent objects such as users, products, orders, or content records without requiring every record to have exactly the same set of fields.
A simplified relational representation:
STUDENT table

x: StudentID | Name | Course
1         | Asha | BCA

b.x: A document-style representation may look like:

x: "studentId": 1,
"name": "Asha",
"course": "BCA"

b.x: This is illustrative JSON-like syntax. MongoDB stores BSON internally, which supports additional data types beyond standard JSON.
15.2 Main concepts
Database
A container for collections and other database objects.
Collection
A group of documents, broadly comparable to a table in some use cases, but documents need not all have identical fields unless schema validation or application rules require it.
Document
A record consisting of field-value pairs, potentially including nested documents and arrays.
Field
A named value within a document.
_id
A special field used as the document's identifier. MongoDB creates an ObjectId by default when an identifier is not supplied, although other identifier types can be used.
15.3 Example document

x: "name": "Asha",
"course": "BCA",
"skills": ["Python", "SQL"],
"address": {
"city": "Lucknow",
"country": "India"

b.x: This document contains simple fields, an array, and a nested document.
15.4 Basic MongoDB operations
MongoDB operations commonly follow the CRUD model

x: Create: insert documents.
Read: find matching documents.
Update: change fields or documents.
Delete: remove documents.

b.x: Illustrative shell commands:

x: db.students.insertOne({
name: "Asha",
course: "BCA"
db.students.find({ course: "BCA" })
db.students.updateOne(
{ $set: { course: "BCA - Semester 1" } }
db.students.deleteOne({ _id: 101 })

b.x: These commands illustrate the MongoDB shell style. They should be tested in a suitable development database, not blindly copied into a production environment.
15.5 Flexible schema
Documents in a collection may have different fields. This flexibility is useful when records naturally vary, but it can also create inconsistent data if no validation is applied.

For example, one document may use age as a number while another stores it as text. Applications can then encounter unexpected behavior. Schema validation, consistent application models, and migration procedures help manage this risk.
15.6 Embedding and referencing
Embedding
Store related information inside the same document.

x: an order document may contain a small array of line items.

b.x: Advantages

x: Related data can be retrieved together.
Some operations can be simpler.
It can reduce the need for joins or multiple requests.

b.x: Limitations

x: Documents can become large.
Duplicated embedded facts can become inconsistent.
Frequently changing shared data may be awkward.

b.x: Referencing
Store a reference to another document, such as a customer identifier in an order.
Advantages

x: Shared information can be stored once.
Separate entities can be updated independently.

b.x: Limitations

x: Related data may require additional queries or lookup operations.
Application logic may need to coordinate multiple documents.

b.x: Choose embedding or referencing according to the relationship, update patterns, and query workload.
15.7 Indexes

Indexes help MongoDB locate documents more efficiently for supported queries. They can improve read performance but consume storage and add overhead to writes because index entries must be maintained.
Indexes should be selected based on real query patterns. Too many indexes can make inserts and updates more expensive.
15.8 MongoDB security considerations

x: Enable authentication and configure appropriate authorization.
Use least-privilege roles.
Restrict network exposure.
Use TLS for network connections.
Protect database files and backups.
Keep software updated.
Monitor failed logins and administrative changes.
Avoid embedding secrets in documents or source code.
Validate application inputs.
Test restore procedures.

b.x: A flexible document schema does not remove the need for data validation and access control.

sec.s: Apache Cassandra is a distributed wide-column database designed for high availability and large-scale data…

b.x: 16.1 What is Apache Cassandra?

Apache Cassandra is a distributed wide-column database designed for high availability and large-scale data workloads across multiple nodes. It is often used for event data, time-series-like workloads, large operational datasets, and applications that need distributed write capacity.

Cassandra uses a data model and query language known as CQL (Cassandra Query Language), whose syntax resembles SQL in many respects. However, Cassandra's data modeling and query capabilities are designed around its distributed architecture and query patterns; it is not a relational DBMS with every traditional SQL feature.
16.2 Distributed architecture
A Cassandra deployment may spread data across multiple nodes. Data is partitioned using a partition key and replicated according to the configured replication strategy.
Partitioning
Determines which part of the cluster is responsible for particular data.
Replication
Maintains copies of data on multiple nodes to improve resilience and availability.
Coordinator
A node that handles a client request and coordinates with the relevant replicas. In typical Cassandra architecture, nodes can accept client requests rather than relying on one permanent master node.
16.3 Key concepts
Keyspace
A top-level namespace containing tables and related configuration, including replication settings.
Table
A structure with defined columns and a primary key.
Partition key
The part of the primary key that determines data partitioning.
Clustering columns
Key components that determine ordering within a partition, according to the table's definition.
Replication factor
The number of replicas maintained for data under the relevant replication configuration.
Consistency level
A setting that determines how many replicas must respond successfully to a read or write operation. The available levels and exact semantics depend on the operation and configuration.
16.4 Data modeling

Cassandra data models should be designed around the queries the application needs to execute. Unlike a conventional relational design where normalization and joins are central, Cassandra commonly uses denormalized tables that may duplicate data to support efficient access patterns.

For example, an application that needs recent events by user might create a table whose partition key includes UserID and whose clustering columns order events by time. The precise schema must account for partition size, access patterns, write distribution, and query requirements.
16.5 Illustrative CQL table

x: CREATE KEYSPACE learning
WITH replication = {
'class': 'SimpleStrategy',
'replication_factor': 1
CREATE TABLE learning.student_events (
student_id int,
event_time timestamp,
event_type text,
details text,
PRIMARY KEY (student_id, event_time)

b.x: This is a teaching example for a single-node or simple learning environment. Production deployments need an appropriate replication strategy for their topology, security configuration, capacity planning, and tested recovery procedures. SimpleStrategy is generally not the recommended strategy for a multi-datacenter production deployment.
16.6 Availability and scaling

Cassandra is designed to distribute data and operations across nodes. Adding nodes can increase capacity, but scaling still requires operational planning, appropriate partitioning, replication management, monitoring, and maintenance.

A distributed system is not automatically resilient to every failure. Incorrect replication settings, network partitions, overloaded nodes, bad schema design, or operator mistakes can still cause availability or data-quality problems.
16.7 Consistency choices

Cassandra supports tunable consistency for operations. The number of replicas required to acknowledge a read or write affects latency, availability, and the likelihood of reading the latest write under the relevant failure conditions.
For a simplified single-data-center replication factor RF, a common quorum condition is:
R + W > RF

where R is the number of replica responses required for a read and W is the number required for a write. Under appropriate assumptions, this overlap helps ensure that a quorum read intersects a quorum write. This rule is not a universal guarantee of all application-level consistency properties; details depend on configuration, failure scenarios, and the consistency levels used.
16.8 Cassandra security considerations

x: Enable authentication and authorization.
Use network encryption for client and node-to-node traffic where required.
Restrict access to cluster nodes.
Protect credentials and certificates.
Configure replication and backups carefully.
Monitor node health, query patterns, and authentication events.
Use supported versions and secure configurations.
Test node-failure and recovery procedures.

sec.s: Neither system is universally superior.

x: Feature | MongoDB | Apache Cassandra
Primary model | Document database | Distributed wide-column database
Typical record | BSON document | Row organized by partition and clustering keys
Schema | Flexible document structure, with optional validation | Table schema designed around partition keys and query patterns
Query interface | MongoDB query and aggregation APIs | CQL and supported data-access mechanisms
Common strengths | Nested documents, application objects, flexible data structures | Distributed write workloads, large datasets, high availability
Data modeling | Embedding and referencing | Query-oriented, often denormalized tables
Distribution | Supports sharding and replication | Distributed partitioning and replication are central design concepts
Consistency | Depends on read/write concerns, transactions, and deployment settings | Tunable consistency levels for operations
Best fit | Workloads that fit document retrieval and document updates | Workloads that fit known partition-oriented access patterns at distributed scale

b.x: Neither system is universally superior. A fair comparison must consider the actual workload, query requirements, consistency expectations, operational environment, and cost.

sec.s: Distributed databases store or replicate data across multiple machines connected by a network.

b.x: 18.1 Background

Distributed databases store or replicate data across multiple machines connected by a network. A network partition occurs when some nodes cannot communicate with other nodes, even though each side may still be running.
The CAP theorem is a result about the guarantees a distributed data system can provide when a network partition occurs.
CAP stands for

x: Consistency.
Availability.
Partition tolerance.

b.x: The theorem is often summarized as saying that, when a partition occurs, a distributed system must choose between providing linearizable consistency and ensuring that every request to a non-failing node receives a successful response. This is more precise than saying that a system can “only ever choose two out of three” in every situation.
18.2 Consistency in CAP
In the CAP context, consistency usually means a strong, linearizable view of a single-copy system: operations behave as if they occurred atomically in an order consistent with real time.

This is not exactly the same as the “Consistency” in ACID. ACID consistency concerns preserving database constraints and valid states. CAP consistency is a distributed-systems guarantee about how reads and writes appear across replicas.
18.3 Availability in CAP

Availability means that every request received by a non-failing node eventually returns a response, although that response may not reflect the latest write if the system chooses an availability-oriented behavior during a partition.
This definition is stronger and more specific than general service uptime. In practice, systems also consider latency, partial failures, request types, and operational availability.
18.4 Partition tolerance

Partition tolerance means the system continues to operate in the presence of a communication failure that separates parts of the distributed system. In real distributed environments, network partitions cannot simply be assumed never to happen.
18.5 CP and AP behavior during a partition
CP-style behavior
The system preserves the required strong consistency guarantee by rejecting or delaying some operations on nodes that cannot safely coordinate.
AP-style behavior
The system continues responding to requests on reachable sides of the partition, potentially accepting divergent or stale states that must later be reconciled according to its design.
These are simplified categories. Actual products can offer configurable consistency levels and different behavior for different operations.
18.6 What about CA?

In an idealized model with no network partition, a system can provide consistency and availability. However, in a genuinely distributed environment where partitions are possible, a design cannot guarantee both strong consistency and full availability during every partition. A single-node system avoids some network-partition issues but has different failure and availability limits.
18.7 Example
Imagine two replicas, Node A and Node B, holding a user's account balance. The network link between them fails.
A client sends a withdrawal to Node A while another client tries to read or update the account through Node B.
A consistency-first approach may refuse or delay operations that cannot be safely coordinated, avoiding conflicting accepted updates.
An availability-first approach may continue accepting operations on both sides. It must then deal with conflicting changes or stale reads when communication is restored.

For financial balances, accepting conflicting withdrawals may be unacceptable. For some social-media reactions or telemetry events, temporary divergence may be an acceptable trade-off. The correct choice depends on business rules.
18.8 CAP does not mean “choose any two forever”

The theorem is about the trade-off during a partition. It does not mean a database can freely turn off consistency or availability at all times. Many systems provide strong guarantees when communication is healthy and change behavior only under particular failure conditions.
Also, “consistency” in CAP should not be confused with ACID consistency, and “availability” in CAP is a formal property rather than a casual statement that a service is usually online.

sec.s: Big Data refers to datasets and data-processing workloads whose scale, speed, or complexity makes…

b.x: 19.1 What is Big Data?
Big Data refers to datasets and data-processing workloads whose scale, speed, or complexity makes traditional tools or architectures insufficient or impractical for the required task.
Big Data is not defined by one fixed file size. What counts as “big” depends on available hardware, workload, response-time requirements, data formats, and organizational capabilities.
19.2 The 3 Vs
Volume
The amount of data generated, stored, and processed.

x: billions of event records generated by a large application.

b.x: Velocity
The speed at which data arrives and needs to be processed.

x: sensor measurements or financial events arriving continuously.

b.x: Variety
The diversity of data formats.
Examples include structured relational records, JSON documents, logs, images, audio, and text.
19.3 Additional Vs
Veracity
The reliability and quality of the data. Big datasets may contain duplicates, missing values, noise, or inaccurate records.
Value
The useful insight or business outcome obtained from data.
Variability
Changes in data rate, structure, or meaning over time.
These additional Vs are common conceptual extensions, not a single mandatory formal definition.
19.4 Examples of Big Data

x: Web and application event logs.
IoT sensor readings.
E-commerce clickstream data.
Scientific measurements.
Large-scale image or video collections.
Financial market events.
Search and recommendation activity.
Large public datasets used for research.

b.x: 19.5 Big Data challenges
Storage
Keeping large datasets safely and economically.
Processing
Executing transformations and analyses within required time limits.
Data quality
Handling missing, duplicated, or inconsistent records.
Governance
Defining ownership, retention, access, and permitted use.
Security and privacy
Protecting personal and sensitive information across distributed systems.
Cost
Managing storage, compute, network transfer, and operational complexity.
Integration
Combining data from many formats and systems.
Reliability
Handling node failures, task failures, and partial data corruption.

sec.s: Large datasets may be stored across multiple machines or in scalable object-storage systems.

b.x: 20.1 Distributed file systems and object storage
Large datasets may be stored across multiple machines or in scalable object-storage systems.
Hadoop Distributed File System (HDFS)
A distributed file system designed to store large files across a cluster, with mechanisms for distributing blocks and maintaining replicas according to its configuration.
Object storage

Stores data as objects in a scalable service or storage system. It is often used for data lakes, backups, archives, and analytics inputs. Object storage is not the same as a conventional mounted file system, although applications can access it through APIs or compatible interfaces.
20.2 Apache Hadoop
Apache Hadoop is an ecosystem for distributed storage and processing of large datasets. It is historically associated with HDFS, YARN for resource management, and MapReduce for batch processing.
MapReduce

A programming model that divides work into mapping and reducing stages. The map stage transforms input records into intermediate key-value pairs. The reduce stage aggregates or combines values associated with keys.
Hadoop remains important historically and in some deployments, although many modern analytics platforms use other processing engines and cloud services.
20.3 Apache Spark
Apache Spark is a distributed processing engine used for batch data processing, SQL analytics, streaming-oriented workloads, and machine-learning-related processing.

Spark can execute work across a cluster and optimize data transformations. It is not itself a general-purpose replacement for every operational database. It often reads from and writes to storage systems, data lakes, databases, and message platforms.
20.4 Apache Kafka
Apache Kafka is a distributed event-streaming platform used to publish, store, and consume streams of events.
Example flow
Application events → Kafka topics → stream processing → data lake or analytical database.

Kafka can help decouple producers and consumers. It does not automatically guarantee that every downstream business process is correct; applications must design for retries, duplicate processing, ordering needs, and delivery semantics.
20.5 Stream processing
Batch processing handles collections of data over a bounded period or dataset.
Stream processing handles continuously arriving events, often with low-latency requirements.
Examples

x: Batch: calculate yesterday's total sales.
Streaming: detect a potentially fraudulent payment within seconds.

b.x: Some systems support both approaches. Real stream-processing design must consider event time, late-arriving data, duplicate events, state management, and recovery.
20.6 Data lake and data warehouse
Data lake
A storage environment that can retain raw or lightly processed data in multiple formats for different uses.
Data warehouse
A curated analytical system designed to support reporting, business intelligence, and structured analysis.
The boundary can be blurred in modern architectures. Both require governance, data-quality controls, access policies, and cost management.
20.7 ETL and ELT
ETL means Extract, Transform, Load

x: Extract data from sources.
Transform it into the required form.
Load it into the destination.

b.x: ELT means Extract, Load, Transform

x: Extract data.
Load it into a target platform.
Transform it within that platform.

b.x: The choice depends on processing capabilities, data governance, latency, and architecture.
20.8 Big Data architecture example
A simplified architecture:
1. Data sources
Applications, sensors, transactions, websites, and external feeds.
2. Ingestion
Batch imports or event streams.
3. Storage
Data lake, object storage, distributed file system, or suitable databases.
4. Processing
Batch engine or stream-processing engine.
5. Serving
Analytical database, search index, dashboard service, or application API.
6. Governance and security
Identity, permissions, encryption, lineage, retention, quality checks, and monitoring across the pipeline.
20.9 Big Data security

x: Apply least privilege to storage and processing services.
Encrypt data at rest and in transit.
Avoid storing unnecessary personal data.
Restrict access to raw and curated datasets.
Monitor data exports and permission changes.
Manage service credentials and keys securely.
Apply retention and deletion policies.
Track data lineage and transformations.
Validate data before using it for high-impact decisions.
Test backup and disaster-recovery processes.

sec.s: Increase the resources of one machine, such as CPU, memory, or storage capacity.

b.x: 21.1 Horizontal and vertical scaling
Vertical scaling
Increase the resources of one machine, such as CPU, memory, or storage capacity.
Horizontal scaling
Add more machines or nodes and distribute work across them.

Vertical scaling can be simpler but has hardware and capacity limits. Horizontal scaling can support larger workloads but introduces networking, replication, partitioning, coordination, and failure-management challenges.
21.2 Sharding and partitioning
Partitioning divides a dataset into smaller pieces. Sharding commonly refers to distributing partitions across multiple servers or nodes.
Possible partition keys include

x: User identifier.
Tenant identifier.
Time range.
Geographic region.
A hash of an identifier.

b.x: A poor partition key can create hotspots, where one node receives a disproportionate amount of traffic or data. Good partitioning should consider both data distribution and query patterns.
21.3 Replication
Replication keeps multiple copies of data. It can improve availability and read capacity, and it can help with recovery from node failure.
Replication introduces questions such as

x: Which copy is authoritative for a write?
When is a write considered committed?
How stale may a replica be?
How are conflicting changes resolved?
What happens during a network partition?
How is a failed replica brought up to date?

b.x: Replication is not the same as a backup. It can copy accidental changes and corruption to all replicas.
21.4 Consistency models
Strong consistency
A read reflects the latest completed write according to the system's defined consistency model.
Eventual consistency
If no new updates occur and the system can communicate and converge, replicas are expected eventually to converge to a consistent state. Reads may temporarily return stale values.
Other models provide intermediate or operation-specific guarantees. The exact definition and guarantees depend on the system.
21.5 Distributed transactions

A transaction involving multiple services or databases is more complicated than a transaction within one database. Distributed transaction protocols may coordinate commits, while application-level workflows may use compensating actions or sagas.

A single local database transaction cannot automatically make an external API call, payment processor, and another database atomic. Systems must design explicit failure handling for such cross-system workflows.

sec.s: A blockchain is a type of distributed ledger in which records are grouped into blocks, and each block…

b.x: 22.1 Definition

A blockchain is a type of distributed ledger in which records are grouped into blocks, and each block typically includes a cryptographic hash linking it to a previous block. Participants follow a protocol to agree on the ledger's accepted history.
A blockchain can be permissionless, where participation is broadly open under the protocol's rules, or permissioned, where participation and validation are restricted to approved entities.
Blockchain systems combine several ideas

x: Cryptographic hashes.
Digital signatures.
Replicated ledger data.
A protocol for ordering or accepting transactions.
A consensus or agreement mechanism.
Incentives or governance rules in some designs.

b.x: 22.2 What is a ledger?

A ledger is a record of transactions or events. A conventional database may maintain a ledger table as well, but a blockchain ledger is distributed among participants and uses cryptographic linking and protocol rules to coordinate accepted history.
22.3 Why blockchain is described as tamper-resistant

Each block commonly contains a hash of its contents and a reference to the preceding block's hash. If the contents of an earlier block change, its hash changes and the subsequent link no longer matches.

In many blockchain systems, changing an accepted historical record also requires overcoming the network's consensus or validation rules. This makes unauthorized alteration difficult under the system's security assumptions.

“Tamper-proof” is an oversimplification. A blockchain is better described as tamper-resistant or tamper-evident. Security depends on the consensus mechanism, distribution of control, software correctness, cryptographic assumptions, governance, and the attacker's resources.
22.4 Cryptographic hash
A cryptographic hash function takes input data and produces a fixed-length digest.
Desirable properties include

x: It is computationally difficult to find an input that produces a chosen digest.
It is difficult to find two different inputs with the same digest.
A small input change causes a substantially different digest.

b.x: A hash is not encryption: it does not use a decryption key to recover the original content.
22.5 Digital signatures

Digital signatures use asymmetric cryptography to help verify that a message or transaction was authorized by the holder of a corresponding private key and that the signed content has not been altered in a way that invalidates the signature.
A signature does not automatically prove the real-world identity of a person. Identity binding depends on how keys are issued, protected, and associated with participants.
22.6 Blocks and chains
A simplified block may contain

x: A set of transactions.
A timestamp or other ordering metadata.
A reference to the previous block.
A hash or commitment to the block contents.
Consensus-specific information.

b.x: The exact block structure varies across blockchain systems.

sec.s: Not every blockchain uses the same transaction flow, block structure, or consensus mechanism.

b.x: 23.1 How a blockchain transaction works
A simplified workflow is:

x: A participant creates a transaction.
The transaction is signed using the participant's private key where the system uses signatures.
The transaction is broadcast to participating nodes.
Nodes check the transaction against protocol rules.
Valid transactions are selected and ordered into a proposed block or ledger update.
The network's consensus mechanism determines which proposed history is accepted.
Nodes update or extend their ledger state.
Participants treat the transaction as confirmed according to the system's confirmation rules.

b.x: Not every blockchain uses the same transaction flow, block structure, or consensus mechanism. Some use proof of work, some use proof of stake, and permissioned systems may use other agreement protocols.
23.2 Decentralization

Decentralization means that control or validation is distributed across multiple participants rather than held entirely by one central operator. The degree of decentralization varies significantly between systems.
A network can have many nodes but still be highly concentrated if a small number of operators control most validation power, infrastructure, or governance.
23.3 Consensus
Consensus is the process by which participants agree on an accepted ledger state or ordering of transactions despite possible delays or faulty participants.
Different consensus mechanisms make different assumptions about:

x: The number and behavior of faulty participants.
Network timing.
The cost of creating or validating blocks.
Who can participate.
Finality and confirmation time.
Resource usage.

b.x: Proof of work generally relies on computational work and probabilistic confirmation. Proof of stake generally uses stake-related validator selection and protocol penalties or incentives. Permissioned systems may use protocols designed for known validators.
No consensus mechanism is free of trade-offs.
23.4 Smart contracts
A smart contract is code executed according to the rules of a blockchain platform. It can implement rules such as recording a transfer, managing an asset, or enforcing a multi-party workflow.

Smart contracts can reduce dependence on a single operator for certain rule enforcement, but they can contain bugs, interact with unreliable external data, or implement incorrect business logic. A smart contract's execution does not guarantee that its rules are legally correct or that its inputs are truthful.
23.5 Blockchain use cases
Potential applications include

x: Shared records among organizations that do not fully trust one another.
Asset ownership and transfer systems.
Supply-chain event records.
Audit trails where multiple parties need a common history.
Certain digital-identity and credential systems.
Tokenized assets.
Automated workflows implemented through smart contracts.

b.x: A blockchain is most compelling when multiple parties need a shared, verifiable ledger and no single party is ideally positioned to control the whole record. If one trusted organization already manages the data and conventional access controls meet the requirements, a normal database may be simpler, cheaper, and more efficient.
23.6 Limitations
Performance
Consensus and replication can reduce throughput or increase latency compared with a centralized database.
Storage growth
Participants may need to store or validate substantial ledger history, depending on the system.
Privacy
Public ledgers can expose transaction patterns and persistent records. Encryption does not automatically hide metadata or all transaction relationships.
Immutability challenges
Errors may be difficult to correct directly. Systems may append a correcting transaction, but the earlier record can remain visible.
Governance
Upgrades, disputes, and protocol changes require governance mechanisms.
Key loss
If a user loses a private key and no recovery mechanism exists, access to associated assets or permissions may be lost.
Smart-contract bugs
Incorrect code may execute exactly as written and create irreversible consequences.
Centralization
Mining, staking, validation, infrastructure, or governance can become concentrated.
Legal and operational issues
Data protection, retention, accountability, and jurisdictional requirements may be difficult to reconcile with permanent replicated records.

sec.s: Blockchain stores data and can be viewed as a specialized distributed ledger.

x: Feature | Conventional database | Blockchain ledger
Control | Often managed by one organization or a defined administrator group | Shared among network participants to varying degrees
Data changes | Authorized records can usually be updated or deleted according to policy | Accepted history is designed to be difficult to rewrite; corrections often use new entries
Performance | Often high throughput and low latency for suitable workloads | Depends on consensus, replication, and protocol; often has additional overhead
Privacy | Access can be tightly restricted | Public systems may expose data and metadata broadly; permissioned designs differ
Trust model | Users trust the operator, controls, and audit mechanisms | Participants rely on cryptography, consensus, protocol rules, and governance
Recovery | Backups, logs, replicas, and standard recovery procedures | Recovery and fork handling depend on protocol and network design
Best fit | General-purpose storage, queries, updates, and transactional applications | Shared verifiable history among parties needing a common ledger
Administration | Database administrators and organization policies | Network governance, validators, developers, and participant rules

b.x: 24.1 Is blockchain a database?

Blockchain stores data and can be viewed as a specialized distributed ledger. However, it is not equivalent to a general-purpose relational or document database. Many blockchain systems are optimized for ordered, verifiable transactions rather than flexible queries, frequent deletion, and arbitrary record updates.
24.2 When not to use blockchain
A conventional database is often preferable when

x: One trusted organization controls the system.
High write throughput and low latency are critical.
Data must be changed or deleted under ordinary retention policies.
Complex ad hoc queries are central to the application.
Participants do not need a shared consensus process.
The overhead of distributed validation has no clear benefit.

sec.s: A system with strong encryption but weak access control may still expose data to legitimate accounts with…

b.x: 25.1 Security is broader than encryption
A secure database system combines

x: Authentication.
Authorization.
Least privilege.
Encryption at rest and in transit.
Safe application queries.
Auditing and monitoring.
Patching and configuration management.
Backups and tested recovery.
Incident response.

b.x: A system with strong encryption but weak access control may still expose data to legitimate accounts with excessive permissions.
25.2 Privacy by design
Privacy by design means considering data protection from the start rather than adding it only after the system is built.
Practical steps include

x: Collect only necessary data.
Limit who can access sensitive fields.
Use masking or tokenization where suitable.
Define retention and deletion schedules.
Avoid putting personal information into public logs or blockchain records.
Assess whether a dataset can be re-identified when combined with other information.
Provide appropriate transparency and consent mechanisms where required.

b.x: 25.3 Security of NoSQL systems
NoSQL systems still require

x: Authentication.
Authorization.
Network restrictions.
Encryption.
Input validation.
Audit logs.
Secure backups.
Patch management.

b.x: A common mistake is assuming that a NoSQL database is secure simply because it does not use conventional SQL. Misconfigured access, stolen credentials, exposed network ports, and insecure application logic can affect any database category.
25.4 Data governance in Big Data
Large-scale data environments often copy data into multiple systems for processing. Every copy may introduce a new access path and retention risk.
A governance plan should identify

x: Data owner and purpose.
Sensitivity classification.
Authorized users and services.
Origin and transformations.
Retention period.
Deletion or correction requirements.
Data-sharing restrictions.
Monitoring and audit expectations.

b.x: 25.5 Blockchain privacy

Sensitive personal information should not be placed directly on a public blockchain without careful analysis. A record can remain available for a long time, and deleting a private key or changing an application interface does not necessarily remove the historical ledger data.

Some designs store only a cryptographic commitment or reference on-chain and keep sensitive details in a controlled off-chain system. Even then, the commitment, metadata, or linkage may reveal information, so privacy review remains necessary.
25.6 Responsible technology selection
Before choosing a database technology, ask

x: What data must be stored?
What queries and updates are required?
What transaction guarantees are needed?
What scale and latency are expected?
What should happen during network partitions?
Who is allowed to access the data?
How will the system be audited?
What are the backup and recovery requirements?
How will the system be operated and patched?
Does the technology solve a real requirement better than simpler alternatives?

sec.s: The following examples are for learning.

b.x: The following examples are for learning. Exact syntax and behavior depend on the database product and configuration. Run security experiments only in a local or authorized test environment.
26.1 Illustrative SQL role and grant
A simplified SQL example:

x: CREATE ROLE reporting_role;
GRANT SELECT ON Student TO reporting_role;

b.x: The exact support for CREATE ROLE, object privileges, and role membership differs across database systems. The example demonstrates the concept: assign read permission to a role and then grant that role to approved users or accounts using the target DBMS's syntax.
26.2 Illustrative MongoDB query

x: db.students.find(
{ course: "BCA" },
{ name: 1, course: 1, _id: 0 }

b.x: This asks for students whose course is BCA and projects only the name and course fields in the result. Projection can reduce unnecessary data exposure in a query result, but it is not a substitute for authorization.
26.3 Illustrative MongoDB update

x: db.students.updateOne(
{ $set: { course: "BCA" } }

b.x: In an application, verify that the caller is allowed to update the targeted record. A database query that is syntactically correct may still violate application-level authorization if the filter or access policy is inadequate.
26.4 Illustrative Cassandra query

x: SELECT student_id, event_time, event_type
FROM learning.student_events
WHERE student_id = 101;

b.x: This example filters on the partition key student_id. Cassandra queries are designed around the table's primary-key structure. Arbitrary filtering across large distributed datasets may be restricted or expensive, so data modeling should be based on required query patterns.
26.5 Illustrative security audit checklist
For a small learning project

x: Confirm that only intended accounts can connect.
Use a separate application account rather than an administrator account.
Test that read-only users cannot update data.
Test that unauthorized accounts cannot read protected tables.
Require encrypted remote connections where supported.
Check that backup files are protected.
Record login failures and privilege changes where available.
Review logs after intentionally failed test logins.
Keep database credentials out of public repositories.
Verify that the application handles permission errors safely.

b.x: 26.6 Illustrative incident
Scenario
